extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers, students and scholars of moral philosophy, evolution, and ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria and standards Darwin gives for judging actions as moral or immoral, and for explaining the origin and development of conscience and moral sense in humans. Focuses on instincts, sympathy, conscience, social judgment, habit, and the welfare of the community as evaluative touchstones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a moral being
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral being is one who is capable of comparing his past and future actions or motives, and of approving or disapproving of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses this as the key test: lower animals lack the capacity for such reflective comparison, so similar helpful or brave acts by animals are not called moral. This capacity distinguishes moral agency and grounds whether actions are judged moral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impulsive and habitual actions can be moral
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions performed impulsively through instinct, or from long-acquired habit, are regarded as moral when performed by a moral being, not only those done deliberately after a struggle with opposing desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues it is scarcely possible to draw a clear line between deliberate moral acts and instinctive or habitual ones; examples include instantaneous rescues and inherited virtuous dispositions. Both spontaneity and deliberate sacrifice can be counted moral, though overcoming opposing motives often wins special praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength and persistence of instincts determine action
rubrics_metrics.description: Which instinct prevails—social (including love of praise/fear of blame) or self-regarding (self-preservation, hunger, lust, vengeance)—depends on their relative strength and persistence in the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistent social instincts can conquer temporary passions, producing self-sacrifice; conversely, strong self-regarding instincts may prevent moral action. Examples: maternal courage, heroic rescue vs. cowardice due to strong self-preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as retrospective moral judge and future guide
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience looks backwards: after action, comparison of past impressions with persistent social instincts and the judgment of others produces remorse, regret, shame or repentance, and leads to resolutions to act differently in future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin frames conscience primarily as a product of reflection upon past acts judged by social instincts and public opinion; this retrospective feeling then functions to regulate future behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of reflection and sympathy in producing moral feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Man’s mental activity — incessant reflection and the re-passing of past impressions combined with sympathy and knowledge of others’ approbation or blame — creates feelings like regret when selfish impulses have been followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because humans can vividly recall past impressions and judge them in light of sympathy and community opinion, they suffer dissatisfaction when present impulses conflict with enduring social instincts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community judgment (law of honour) shapes conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: The expressed wishes and opinions of the community, and the 'law of honour' (opinion of one’s equals), strongly influence feelings of shame and remorse, sometimes causing agony even when breach of that law accords with true morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes that public opinion can reinforce social instincts but also lead to absurd or harmful customs that the conscience enforces despite their opposition to true welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher vs lower moral rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher moral rules are founded on social instincts and relate to the welfare of others, supported by approbation of fellow-men and by reason; lower rules chiefly relate to self and arise from public opinion matured by experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher rules concern altruistic duties to others (the welfare of the community); lower rules concern self-regarding virtues which may still be valuable but were not originally esteemed by rude tribes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of moral sense: social instincts aided by reason, instruction, and religion
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral sense arises from social instincts and sympathy, which are then extended, cultivated and reinforced by reason, instruction, habit, and reverence or fear of gods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin presents social instincts as primary impulses; subsequent cultural and cognitive processes expand and sophisticate moral sensibilities and norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of morality: general good (welfare) over greatest happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: As a practical standard Darwin prefers the 'general good' or welfare of the community (rearing the greatest number of individuals in full vigour) as the basis for morality, rather than the 'greatest happiness' principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He argues social instincts were developed for the general good rather than mere happiness and suggests using welfare as the moral standard, while noting possible limitations for political ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral sentiments expand with social scale and civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: As small tribes unite into larger communities, individuals should extend their social instincts and sympathies first to nation-members and then, potentially, to all races and eventually to other sentient beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civilisation and sustained practice of moral virtues spread sympathy beyond kin and tribe; sympathy toward lower animals is a late moral acquisition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit, self-command, and possible inheritance of moral tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Long habit and self-command can render social instincts immediately dominant; such habits may be acquired and possibly partially inherited, aiding moral conduct across generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites anecdotal familial tendencies (to steal or lie) and links bodily or mental states to moral tendencies; he allows for partial biological transmission of virtuous or vicious predispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity of remorse depends on multiple factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The depth of regret, shame, repentance or remorse depends on the strength of the violated instinct, the strength of the temptation, the judgment of one’s fellows, and reverence or fear of gods or spirits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin responds to critics who doubt naturalistic accounts of deep remorse by pointing to these interacting causes; cultural and religious context can amplify remorse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive morality is tribe-centered
rubrics_metrics.description: In rude societies, actions are judged good or bad solely by how they affect the welfare of the tribe; virtues are practised almost exclusively in relation to tribe-members and crimes against outsiders may not be reproached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include scalping, slavery, infanticide and ritual practices that are not condemned within a tribe; moral expansion beyond the tribe requires reasoning, broader sympathy, and social change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions judged by their effect on tribe welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief criterion for moral judgment in early man was whether acts preserved coherence and utility for the tribe (obedience, courage, fidelity), rather than abstract individual rights or universal principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin emphasizes practical tribal necessities (e.g., courage, self-sacrifice, fidelity) as the virtues most honoured in primitive societies; self-regarding virtues were less prized.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Ought' as consciousness of a rule of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The imperative 'ought' denotes merely the consciousness of a rule of conduct (regardless of its origin), indicating that habituation or learned rules give rise to a felt duty to act accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses examples ('a pointer ought to point') to show that 'ought' reflects internalized rules and habits rather than an inherently metaphysical moral faculty.
